ledeHtml: the Japan that rose on policy, record profits and ¥25.7tn of buyback frames — TOPIX +14.40% over twelve months, the Nikkei +20.52% — and the Japan that fell −22.0% from its June record into 20 November and was rescued, in part, by a board vote in Santa Clara. This report measures both: all 33 TOPIX sectors, the 54-name coverage universe name by name, the US as one comparison block, and the reasons — earnings, guidance revisions, dilution, governance — behind every large move. Part 5 is the forward view, labelled J-Core view: which laggards have a dated catalyst to close the gap, which are cheap for a reason, and which leaders are extended.

blocks.heading: Part 1 — The year in one story
1. Market overview — a policy-and-AI year, decided in November
blocks.html: TOPIX rose +14.40% over the twelve months to 24 Nov 2026 (3,290.89 → 3,764.88) and the Nikkei 225 +20.52% (48,659.52 → 58,644.63); for calendar 2026 YTD the gains are +10.44% and +16.50%. The path mattered more than the endpoints (Figure 2). The year opened on the Takaichi policy trade and accelerated after the LDP's February 2026 landslide (316 seats; Nikkei +3.89% on 9 Feb; February +10.36% for the month), then broke on the Iran war: by 23 Mar TOPIX had fallen more than 10% from its 27 Feb record, with Brent above $115. The 8 Apr ceasefire started the fastest recovery of the year — TOPIX regained its high in 41 trading days — and the Nikkei closed above 69,000 for the first time on 15 Jun (69,317.50) after the US–Iran memorandum. The window's highest close was 72,366.34 on 25 Jun 2026 (TOPIX's own peak close, 4,183.56, came later, on 6 Oct). Summer brought a yen crisis instead: USD/JPY touched 163.988 intraday on 22 Jul, and ¥15.39tn of intervention followed between 30 Jul and 3 Aug (more than ¥27tn across 2026), including joint US–Japan action on 31 Jul. Policy tightened in sync in September. November then re-priced the AI complex in nine sessions: Jensen Huang's resignation (announced 12 Nov), an Asia chip rout, Tokyo's −5.06% fall on 20 Nov — the Nikkei's trough close at 56,436.65, −22.0% from the June record — reports of an SEC examination of Nvidia, and finally Huang's unanimous reinstatement on 23 Nov, which drove the +3.91% rebound to 58,644.63 on 24 Nov. The year's returns are therefore a policy-and-earnings story with a positioning accident at the end of it, not a demand collapse: no coverage guidance cut or capex cut drove the November fall. The policy frame: the BOJ raised its rate three times, 0.50% → 1.25% (19 Dec 2025, 16 Jun 2026, 18 Sep 2026); the Fed cut once (10 Dec 2025, to 3.50–3.75%), held five times under new chair Warsh (from 22 May 2026), then hiked back to 3.75–4.00% on 16 Sep 2026. Foreign investors were the marginal buyer: +¥10,490bn net in 2026 to 13 Nov (JPX trading-by-investor-type data), roughly double the whole of 2025. Corporate Japan supplied the earnings: H1 FY2026 net profit was a record ¥35.75tn (+26%), with electrical equipment +96%, and buyback frames reached ¥25.7tn by 13 Nov 2026 (Nomura tally).

blocks.heading: 2. The year month by month — rhythm, breadth, drawdowns and flows
blocks.html: The rhythm of the year. Twelve months, three regimes (Figure 15). TOPIX's best month was February 2026 (+10.44%) on the LDP landslide; its worst was March (−11.19%) in the Iran war break. The Nikkei's extremes were wider — best April (+16.10%) on the ceasefire recovery, worst March (−13.23%) — and the two indices disagreed most in July (TOPIX +0.21%, Nikkei −8.14%), when the yen crisis hit the export- and chip-heavy Nikkei far harder than the broad index. No month after August added more than +3.9% to either index: the year's gains were made by August, defended in September–October, and partially surrendered in November (−5.05% TOPIX, −7.34% Nikkei to 24 Nov). Breadth and dispersion. This was a two-tier market. In the coverage universe, 38 of 54 names were positive over 12M and 32 of 54 YTD, but the median return (+12.8% 12M, +5.4% YTD) sat below TOPIX (+14.4% / +10.4%), and only 24 of the 52 names with a meaningful spread beat TOPIX over 12M — the index was carried by its heavyweights. Dispersion was wide: the coverage interquartile range was 30.5pt (12M) and 27.0pt (YTD), against a full range of 134pt. Sector breadth was healthier — 28 of 33 sectors positive over 12M on the October basis, median +12.5% / +8.8%, IQR 21.9pt / 17.5pt — so the year's extremes were stock-specific (guidance revisions, dilution, governance), not sector-wide. Drawdowns. Correcting the record (Section 13): the Nikkei's record close was 72,366.34 on 25 Jun 2026, and its peak-to-trough fall to 56,436.65 on 20 Nov was −22.0% — the window's largest drawdown, larger than the March war break (TOPIX −11.19% month-end to month-end). TOPIX fell −12.2% from its peak close of 4,183.56 on 6 Oct 2026 (a secondary series, labelled as such in Section 13) to 3,674.22 — roughly three-fifths of the Nikkei's fall, because the crash was concentrated in the price-weighted chip and AI names. The 24 Nov rebound recovered only +3.91% (Nikkei) and +2.47% (TOPIX) off the trough. Flows, bonds and the yen. Foreign investors were the marginal buyer but a pro-cyclical one: +¥10,490bn net in 2026 to 13 Nov, of which +¥9,702bn (92%) came in H1; April's +¥5,339bn was the largest month, and March's −¥2,281bn was selling into the trough. The 10-year JGB yield rose roughly 100bp across the window, from ≈1.8% to a high of 3.111% on 7 Oct 2026, before rallying to ≈2.7–2.8% by 24 Nov as equities fell. USD/JPY ranged 152.09–163.988; the ¥15.39tn intervention of 30 Jul–3 Aug (including joint US–Japan action on 31 Jul) capped the yen crisis, and the pair ended the window at 159.01, only +1.32% weaker — the year's equity story was not an FX story.

blocks.heading: 3. TOPIX-33 sectors — financials and transport led; the rate losers lagged
blocks.html: Sector levels for 24 Nov 2026 are 未取得 for all 33 TOPIX sectors: JPX publishes daily sector values only in its Monthly Statistics Report, and the November edition appears in early December 2026 (Section 13 gives the completion route). The rankings below therefore run to 30 Oct 2026, the latest official month-end, on which basis TOPIX itself was +20.49% (12M) and +16.31% (YTD). November was a down month (TOPIX −5.05% from the October month-end to 24 Nov), so end-November rankings will differ in level, though the leadership structure is unlikely to invert. The year's leadership was financial and logistical, not technological. Marine Transportation (+63.26%), Services (+60.20%), Insurance (+51.29%) and Banks (+47.98%) led the 12M table. Banks were the rate trade delivered in earnings: three BOJ hikes steepened domestic margins, and the three megabanks raised full-year net-profit targets on 13 Nov 2026 (MUFG ¥2.8tn, SMFG ¥1.9tn, Mizuho ¥1.6tn) and added ¥620bn of combined buybacks. Insurers' core profit rose +22% to ¥2.9tn on investment returns. Wholesale Trade (+29.04%) rode the trading houses — Berkshire Hathaway above 10% in all five sogo shosha, all five growing H1 profit and four raising guidance. Nonferrous Metals (+39.37%) is the cable complex's sector line — its internal split is the company story of Section 7. Electric Appliances (+28.39%) carried the AI-capex profit pool (H1 electrical-equipment net profit +96%) yet ranked only eighth: the sector's giants round-tripped hardest into November. The laggards were the rate losers and the tariff takers: Other Products (−12.91%), Construction (−6.07% over 12M; −9.76% YTD, the YTD worst) and Real Estate (−2.79%; −5.77% YTD) — three hikes repriced domestic duration — and Transportation Equipment (+0.31% over 12M; −5.25% YTD), where FY3/26 operating profit fell more than 40% on US tariffs (Toyota alone took a ¥1.38tn hit) before an H1 recovery carried largely by ¥685bn of FX gains. Machinery (+5.24%) is the quiet puzzle of the table: record orders and the year's biggest guidance upgrades sat inside a mid-table sector return, because the upgrades were concentrated in smaller names while the heavy-defence names de-rated (Section 7).

blocks.heading: 4. All 33 sectors — the drivers, sector by sector
blocks.html: 1. Marine Transportation (+63.3% 12M / +56.0% YTD). The Strait of Hormuz closure lengthened voyages and pushed tanker, dry-bulk and container rates sharply higher through 2026 — JCR's 14 May 2026 review already flagged VLCC rates surging on the closure, and by November the three majors were upgrading: NYK's H1 net profit rose 107% to ¥203.5bn with its full-year forecast raised to ¥330bn and its dividend lifted from ¥240 to ¥330, while MOL raised its full-year net-profit forecast 25% to ¥300bn on 2 Nov 2026. The index path matches a rate story, not a one-off spike: +15.2% in July and +17.2% in August 2026 as the disruption persisted. Sources: [JCR, 14 May 2026](https://www.jcr.co.jp/download/91a171c8e5803589583a98838e8ebf158307599e78e0380fa5/2605_KR_ShippingCompanies.pdf); [Tokyo Brief on MOL H1](https://tokyobrief.com/articles/mitsui-osk-lines-half-year-profit-gulf-assumption). 2. Services (+60.2% / +51.4%). The sector's largest name did the work: Recruit Holdings (2.60% of TOPIX at 30 Oct 2026, the sector's anchor weight) reported record Q1 FY2026 results on 7 Aug 2026 — revenue +18.9% YoY to ¥1.04tn with guidance raised — and followed with H1 revenue +19.3% and operating profit +63.9%, plus ¥178.1bn of buybacks executed by 31 Oct 2026. The index jumped +18.3% in May and +20.2% in August 2026, consistent with the HR-technology earnings revisions rather than with the broader market. Source: [Recruit Holdings Q2 FY2026 summary](https://recruit-holdings.com/en/ir/library/upload/Recruit_202703Q2_summary_en.html). 3. Insurance (+51.3% / +39.0%). Insurers were the second leg of the rate trade: three BOJ hikes lifted investment returns, and sector core profit rose 22% to ¥2.9tn (Section 3), helped by continued cross-shareholding sales at high market levels. The path was the steadiest of the leaders — positive in nine of eleven months, including +14.2% in February 2026 and +12.1% in July 2026 — which fits an earnings-and-returns story rather than a single event. 4. Banks (+48.0% / +36.5%). This was the rate trade delivered in earnings: the BOJ's three hikes (19 Dec 2025, 16 Jun 2026, 18 Sep 2026; 0.50% → 1.25%) steepened domestic lending margins, and on 13 Nov 2026 the three megabanks raised full-year net-profit targets (MUFG ¥2.8tn, SMFG ¥1.9tn, Mizuho ¥1.6tn) and added ¥620bn of combined buybacks. The path shows the leverage both ways: +13.2% in January 2026, −13.6% in the March 2026 war break, and −9.7% in October 2026 as the market de-rated into November. 5. Nonferrous Metals (+39.4% / +29.4%). This is the cable complex's sector line: Fujikura's H1 operating profit was a record ¥235bn (+161%) and Furukawa Electric's tripled to ¥57.6bn (+201.1%) on data-centre optical demand, with Furukawa raising guidance twice (Sections 6–7). The sector rose +47.7% in February 2026 alone, then de-rated as a group from June — −23.5% in July and −21.6% in October 2026 — as the market began pricing 2027–28 fibre-capacity additions against shortage pricing. 6. Oil & Coal Products (+34.3% / +25.2%). The war premium is the story: the sector gained +14.8% in January and +13.4% in February 2026 as Middle East risk built, and Brent above $115 by 23 Mar 2026 lifted refining margins and inventory valuations. Unlike most cyclicals it held most of the gain after the 8 Apr 2026 ceasefire (only −8.0% in April, then broadly flat), which is why it finished sixth despite no domestic-demand driver. 7. Wholesale Trade (+29.0% / +20.0%). The trading houses carried the sector: Berkshire Hathaway moved above 10% in all five sogo shosha, all five grew H1 profit and four raised guidance (Section 3). Their energy and metals books also benefited from the same war-driven commodity prices that lifted Oil & Coal and Mining in February–March 2026, when the sector rose +17.6% (February) before giving back −6.0% (March). 8. Electric Appliances (+28.4% / +23.9%). The AI-capex profit pool was real — H1 FY2026 electrical-equipment net profit rose 96% market-wide, Advantest's H1 operating profit rose 96.5% with guidance raised 54.1% on 28 Oct 2026, and Tokyo Electron's first full-year guide (30 Oct 2026) implied operating profit +87.1% with a ¥150bn buyback. But the sector round-tripped hardest: −15.6% in March 2026, −9.2% in October 2026, and the November AI crash after the window — which is why the year's biggest profit pool ranked only eighth. 9. Mining (+27.0% / +27.6%). A near-pure energy-price line: the sector rose +18.1% in March 2026 — the war month, when TOPIX fell about 11% — as Brent spiked above $115 and Hormuz supply risk priced into upstream earnings. It gave back −11.3% in April and −13.6% in May 2026 as crude normalised after the ceasefire, then recovered with the summer oil price; the YTD return (+27.6%) exceeding the 12M return is the signature of a 2026 event, not a trend. 10. Other Financing Business (+24.6% / +16.9%). Leasing and consumer-credit names re-rated with the rest of the financial complex as higher yen rates lifted asset yields and record equity-market levels (Nikkei first above 69,000 on 15 Jun 2026) raised the value of investment and exit portfolios. The path was financial-like: +15.9% in February 2026 and −14.3% in March 2026. A constituent-level earnings attribution for this sector is 未取得. 11. Chemicals (+23.9% / +19.0%). The sector rose with the February 2026 policy trade (+15.2%) and again in May 2026 (+10.4%), and it absorbed the war shock (−10.3% in March) better than most cyclicals, consistent with semiconductor- and AI-materials demand offsetting naphtha cost pressure. H1 FY2026 was a record for corporate Japan overall (net profit ¥35.75tn, +26%), but a chemicals-specific earnings aggregate is 未取得, so the materials-demand driver should be read as market context, not as a verified sector print. 12. Glass & Ceramics Products (+20.7% / +17.1%). The path was the most volatile of the mid-table: +20.1% in February, +16.7% in April and +16.2% in May 2026, then −16.1% in July and −7.8% in October 2026. That pattern fits the sector's two halves — electronic glass and AI/data-centre-related materials riding the capex cycle, domestic construction glass exposed to the rate-driven construction downturn (Construction −9.8% YTD) — but a constituent-level split is 未取得. 13. Securities & Commodities Futures (+19.8% / +8.4%). Broker earnings are a geared play on market levels, and levels were records: the Nikkei closed above 69,000 for the first time on 15 Jun 2026 and reached its record close of 72,366.34 on 25 Jun 2026, with Nomura alone 46.19% of the sector index at 30 Oct 2026 (JPX factsheet). The modest YTD (+8.4%) against the strong 12M is the give-back: −14.8% in March 2026 and −6.3% in October 2026, the two market breaks. 14. Foods (+19.0% / +21.1%). The defensive that compounded: the sector was positive in eight of eleven months and fell only −5.2% in March 2026, roughly half the market's drop, while price revisions passed earlier cost inflation through to earnings. Its best month, +11.9%, came in February 2026 alongside the broad rally; the YTD return exceeding TOPIX (+16.3%) with low volatility is the whole story — no single dated corporate event was identified, and none is claimed. 15. Metal Products (+15.7% / +8.8%). A capex-beta line: +9.7% in February 2026, −12.7% in the March war break, then +10.2% in April and +18.1% in May 2026 as AI factory and data-centre construction demand fed metal processing and components orders. The second half faded (−9.0% in October 2026) with the broader capex complex. A sector-specific earnings aggregate is 未取得. 16. Pulp & Paper (+14.6% / +6.6%). Almost all of the gain came early — +10.9% in February 2026 — and was partly surrendered in March (−13.0%); from April to October 2026 the sector was essentially flat. A substantiated sector-specific driver (packaging price revisions, pulp prices, or a constituent event) is 未取得; the February move coincides with the market-wide post-election rally and should not be over-attributed. 17. Textiles & Apparels (+12.5% / +10.9%). The path tracked the yen and the market beta of its dominant apparel names: +14.3% in February 2026, −14.8% in March, and +8.2% in August 2026 after the intervention pulled USD/JPY back from the 22 Jul 2026 intraday high of 163.988 — a weaker yen flatters overseas earnings translation while raising import costs. Constituent-level earnings verification for this note is 未取得. 18. Pharmaceutical (+10.4% / +9.7%). A defensive sector in a risk-on, rate-led year: it lagged TOPIX by about 10pt over 12M despite +13.4% in February 2026, and its best relative month was October 2026 (+7.3% while TOPIX fell 3.5%), the classic defensive rotation into a falling market. No sector-wide earnings event was identified in the sources used; a specific drug-pricing or pipeline driver is 未取得. 19. Precision Instruments (+10.4% / +10.9%). The sector ground higher with the least drama of any mid-table name — no month worse than −6.3% (March 2026) — consistent with its medical and measurement mix (endoscopes, testing and semiconductor-adjacent optics) sharing the AI-capex tailwind without the cable complex's multiple expansion. It rose +8.4% in February and +6.1% in April 2026. A constituent-level earnings split is 未取得. 20. Warehousing & Harbor Transportation (+9.6% / +7.6%). Two offsetting stories: port and logistics demand stayed firm as Hormuz rerouting lengthened supply chains (the same disruption that lifted Marine Transportation), while the coverage names diverged — Sumitomo Warehouse +13.6% and Mitsubishi Logistics +9.5% over 12M to 24 Nov 2026, against Mitsui-Soko HD −20.7% after its February 2026 Mitsui Fudosan alliance issued 3,000,000 new shares (about 4% dilution). J-Core initiated on all three warehouse names at Overweight on 24 Nov 2026 on real-estate NAV, a valuation argument the earnings path alone does not explain. 21. Rubber Products (+8.7% / +8.6%). Tyre economics ran through the war: +12.2% in February 2026, then −17.5% in March 2026 — the sector's worst month — as oil-linked raw-material costs spiked with Brent above $115, followed by a +13.6% recovery in July 2026 as costs normalised and price hikes held. US tariff exposure on tyre and auto-parts shipments was the standing offset all year. A constituent-level (Bridgestone versus smaller names) split is 未取得. 22. Information & Communication (+7.2% / +4.6%). The sector lagged because its weight is telecom carriers, not AI hardware: it missed the February 2026 rally (−2.9%), rose +13.6% in May 2026 when the AI complex peaked, and fell −7.4% in October 2026 with it. With the policy rate at 1.25% from 18 Sep 2026, high-dividend defensive telecoms lost their yield advantage to banks and insurers, which is the rotation visible in the table as a whole. 23. Iron & Steel (+5.8% / +0.7%). Effectively flat for 2026: small gains in January–February 2026 (+3.7%, +3.3%), a −12.5% war-month drop in March on energy costs, and no recovery leg thereafter. Weak Asian steel demand and Chinese export pricing were the standing headwinds in market commentary all year, but no verified sector earnings aggregate was obtained — that specific attribution is 未取得. 24. Machinery (+5.2% / +3.6%). Report 70's "quiet puzzle": record orders and the year's largest guidance upgrades (Sodick's guide doubled; FUJI +50.2%; Harmonic Drive +64.5%) sat inside a mid-table return because the upgrades were concentrated in smaller names while the heavy defence names de-rated — Mitsubishi Heavy fell 27.4% over 12M to 24 Nov 2026 despite raising its business-profit guide to ¥600bn on 6 Nov 2026, after H1 defence orders fell 64% YoY. Yaskawa, the tracker's only operating-profit cut (−4.2%, 9 Oct 2026, on a core-system migration), dragged the electrical-machinery end. The sector fell −17.5% in March and −10.7% in October 2026. 25. Air Transportation (+5.1% / +4.0%). The mirror image of Marine: the Hormuz closure that raised shipowners' rates raised airlines' fuel bills — Japan Airlines' H1 fuel costs rose 47% to ¥285.6bn and its EBIT fell 36%. The index rose +11.9% in February 2026 before the war, fell −19.0% in March 2026 (the worst sector that month), and never regained momentum, finishing near flat despite record inbound travel demand. Source: [market wrap, Nov 2026](https://filingreader.com/reports/daily/2026-11-08/hormuz-closure-lifts-japans-shipowners-as-huaxin-bids-us16bn-for-brazilian). 26. Electric Power & Gas (+3.3% / +5.3%). Regulated duration in a hiking cycle: three BOJ hikes to 1.25% (18 Sep 2026) raised funding costs and cut the sector's yield appeal, and war-driven fuel prices squeezed the generators in March 2026 (−4.9%). The offsets were data-centre power demand and nuclear-restart expectations, visible in +14.5% in February and +7.2% in August 2026. A utility-by-utility earnings split is 未取得. 27. Retail Trade (+2.9% / +3.6%). One name's record year against a squeezed sector: Ryohin Keikaku rose 62.5% over 12M to 24 Nov 2026 on a record FY8/26 (operating profit ¥103,436mn, +40.1%, the first above ¥100bn), while real-wage pressure capped the broader discretionary names. The sector rose +9.0% in February 2026, fell −8.2% in March, and its +5.8% in October 2026 was defensive outperformance in a falling market. (Ryohin's online store has been suspended since 6 Nov 2026 after an unauthorised-access incident; the earnings cost is unquantified — post-window for this table.) 28. Transportation Equipment (+0.3% / −5.3%). The tariff taker: FY3/26 operating profit fell more than 40% on US tariffs — Toyota alone took a ¥1.38tn hit — and the H1 FY2027 recovery was carried largely by ¥685bn of FX gains rather than volume (Section 3). The index rose +8.4% in February 2026, fell −16.9% in March and −7.6% in June, and was the only large sector negative on a YTD basis outside the rate losers. 29. Land Transportation (−0.1% / −0.9%). Railways and road freight went nowhere: regulated, domestic and rate-sensitive, the sector had no earnings catalyst to offset three BOJ hikes, and fuel costs from the Hormuz disruption squeezed the trucking names while rail demand was steady but unexciting. It fell −6.9% in March 2026 and its best month was only +7.6% (July 2026). A company-specific driver is 未取得; the flat line is itself the finding. 30. Real Estate (−2.8% / −5.8%). A rate loser, as Section 3 puts it: three hikes repriced domestic duration, raising developers' funding costs and cap-rate assumptions. The path shows the policy trade reversing — +20.8% in February 2026 on the post-election fiscal rally, then −16.1% in March 2026 and further losses in May (−9.6%) as the June hike approached. The contrast with Warehousing (+9.6%), where the same property exposure is backed by logistics earnings, is instructive. 31. Fishery, Agriculture & Forestry (−3.5% / −3.1%). The sector rose +13.6% in February 2026 with the broad rally, then gave it back in March (−9.1%) and April (−7.6%) as war-driven fuel and feed costs hit fishing and food-processing margins, and it never recovered. A substantiated sector-specific earnings driver is 未取得 — no fleet, catch, or constituent earnings aggregate was obtained from the sources used. 32. Construction (−6.1% / −9.8%). The YTD worst sector: +17.9% in February 2026 on post-election public-works expectations, then −15.8% in March and a near-uninterrupted slide from July to October 2026 (−4.7%, −0.7%, −2.2%, −3.8%). Three BOJ hikes raised funding and discount rates while labour and materials costs stayed high — the rate-loser profile of Section 3 — and, unlike Real Estate, there was no asset-value offset the market would pay for. 33. Other Products (−12.9% / −1.7%). The 12M loss was made in a single month: −13.3% in December 2025, before the 2026 window even opened; from January to October 2026 the sector actually recovered (+11.0% in August 2026 was its best month). The specific constituent event behind the December 2025 drop is 未取得 — it is not identified in the JPX statistics or in Report 70's sources, and no explanation is offered here rather than inventing one.

blocks.heading: 5. The coverage universe — guidance revisions wrote the leaderboard
blocks.html: Across the 54 coverage names (Figure 6; price return only, dividends excluded), the median return was +12.8% over 12M and +5.4% YTD; 38 of 54 were positive over 12M and 32 of 54 YTD, against TOPIX +14.40% / +10.44%. The distribution is the story: the top ten gained +36% to +107%, the bottom ten lost −9% to −27%, and the middle was flat. Guidance revisions explain the top of the table almost mechanically. The guidance tracker's largest operating-profit upgrades are the leaderboard: Sodick's guide doubled (+100.0%), Harmonic Drive +64.5%, Advantest +54.1%, FUJI +50.2%, Furukawa Electric +43.2%, Misumi +41.8% — and the tracker's only operating-profit cut among these names, Yaskawa (−4.2%), sits fourth from the bottom on YTD. The second pattern is the round trip: eight of the top ten peaked between May and October and gave back 35–70% into November (Furukawa −69.9% from its 26 May peak; Harmonic Drive −52.6%; Tokyo Electron −43.2%), so the 12M ranking is as much a record of where each name stood when the November shock hit as of the year's earnings. The third pattern: the bottom of the table is not an earnings-collapse list — the three heavy-industry names all raised guidance (Section 7). A note on method: six of the 21 top and bottom names split their shares in the window (Furukawa 10-for-1, Fujikura 6-for-1, Tokyo Electron 5-for-1, Kawasaki Heavy 5-for-1, Sumitomo Electric 4-for-1, Keyence 5-for-1); the price files are split-adjusted across every ex-date, verified day by day, so no peak-to-end gap in this report is a split artefact. Advantech is TWD-denominated and NVIDIA USD-denominated; their vs-TOPIX spreads are shown as — in Figure 6.

rows: Orders did it: record 3Q26 revenue NT$32,440mn (+83% YoY), OP +151%, consolidated book-to-bill 1.64 (North America 2.12) and bookings up five straight quarters; the 4Q26 outlook (US$970–990mn, 4 Nov 2026) was framed by management as conservative, and the fade from the NT$740 peak (5 Oct) is the complex-wide autumn de-rating, with no company-specific negative disclosure found. No full-year guidance exists (quarterly US$ outlook only — guidance tracker).

H1 OP tripled to ¥57.6bn (+201.1%) as Optical Solutions swung from ¥0.7bn to ¥23.6bn of OP, and guidance was raised twice to ¥136,000mn (OP guide +43.2%, latest 9 Nov 2026 — guidance tracker); the stock still fell −69.9% from its ¥6,014 peak (26 May), including −17.1% on 5 Nov and a Goldman Sachs target cut (¥6,400 → ¥4,100, 8 Nov), leaving open how much of the 18.0% optical margin is shortage pricing.

H1 OP rose +89.8% (margin 9.5% → 13.6%) on data-centre demand and the digital-model initiatives, guidance was raised twice to ¥78,000mn (OP guide +41.8%, latest 30 Oct 2026 — guidance tracker), and ¥15,909mn of H1 buybacks plus a dividend raise accompanied the revisions; the 11 Nov peak was set on the eve of the November crash, so the gain is an earnings-revision story.

A record FY8/26 (OP ¥103,436mn, +40.1%, the first year above ¥100bn) and a FY8/27 guide to the first ¥1tn revenue year (OP ¥114,000mn, set 14 Oct 2026, unrevised — guidance tracker) drove the rise; the one negative is post-peak — the MUJI online store has been suspended since 6 Nov 2026 after an unauthorised-access incident (up to ~27.26mn records potentially exposed), with the earnings cost unquantified.

Guidance was raised twice to ¥10,200mn (OP guide +64.5%, latest 11 Nov 2026 — guidance tracker), but off a FY3/26 OP base of only ¥2,568mn; the ¥8,890 July peak and the −52.6% round trip are multiple expansion and compression on a very small profit base, with no guidance cut or negative disclosure found.

H1 OP rose +67.2%, and the first full-year guide — disclosed only on 30 Oct 2026, not a revision (guidance tracker) — put FY3/27 OP at ¥1,169,000mn (+87.1% vs FY3/26), with management framing CY2027 wafer-fab equipment at $210bn or more and a ¥150bn buyback alongside; the −43.2% fall from the 1 Jul peak is the sector path, not a miss. A 5-for-1 split (1 Oct 2026) is adjusted in the prices.

H1 OP was ¥456.8bn (+96.5%, at a 54.0% margin) and guidance was raised twice to ¥967,000mn (OP guide +54.1%, latest 28 Oct 2026 — guidance tracker) on CPU-testing demand from agentic AI, with a ¥280bn buyback at the print; it was also the November crash's purest round trip (−11.1% on 16 Nov, the largest single Nikkei drag on 17 Nov, then more than +14% in the 24 Nov rebound).

Robot Solutions (SMT mounters) drove H1 OP up +250.6% and guidance was raised twice to ¥65,500mn (OP guide +50.2%, latest 5 Nov 2026 — guidance tracker), with a ¥10bn buyback completed on 6 Nov (cancellation 14 Dec); the caveat is visibility — backlog of ¥80,472mn is only ~3.8 months of guided sales.

The OP guide doubled to ¥11,000mn (+100.0%, revisions 7 Aug and 6 Nov 2026 — guidance tracker) on China EDM demand and AI-related injection-moulding machines, beating the 2029 mid-term targets three years early; a ~¥8.8bn secondary offering (a cross-shareholding unwind) was the autumn supply overhang, partly offset by a ¥3bn buyback.

Keyence gives no guidance by policy (guidance tracker), so the 29 Oct 2026 print was the event: H1 sales +34.9% and OP +50.0% at a 55.5% margin, with a 5-for-1 split and a dividend raise announced the same day; whether +34.9% growth is a spike or a step-up remains the open question.
No single dominant event: the stock tracked the machine-tool upcycle, with the OP guide raised once, on 12 Nov 2026, to ¥48,000mn (+31.5% vs the initial ¥36,500mn — guidance tracker).

Three successive OP guide raises, to ¥73,000mn (+30.4% vs the initial ¥56,000mn, latest 13 Nov 2026 — guidance tracker), on advanced-materials/semiconductor demand, partly offset by an Energy & Environment cut on hydrogen-market stagnation, explain the steady outperformance.

The second-largest percentage upgrade in the tracker after the two doublings: the OP guide was raised three times to ¥19,000mn (+90.0% vs the initial ¥10,000mn, latest 11 Nov 2026 — guidance tracker); no company-stated reason was extracted from the November notice, so the driver is the revision chain itself, on PCB-drill demand read-across.

The P&L guide was never revised (OP ¥125,000mn, set 6 Aug 2026 — guidance tracker); the positive signal was the order-intake outlook, raised at Q1 (30 Oct 2026) from ¥300,000–400,000mn to ¥400,000–500,000mn, and the stock tracked the semiconductor-equipment complex.

No single dominant event: the OP guide was raised once, on 12 Nov 2026, to ¥58,000mn (+20.8% — guidance tracker), on strong order intake from buoyant capex demand and a weaker-than-assumed yen, and the stock tracked the machinery sector.

A modest OP guide raise to ¥156,500mn (+4.3%, 28 Jul 2026, on record orders — guidance tracker) supported the 12M gain, but the YTD return is flat: the group total was left unchanged at Q2 (30 Oct 2026, with the FT segment cut inside it), and the name gave back its gains in the autumn semiconductor-equipment de-rating.

A single, late OP guide raise to ¥455,000mn (+4.4%, 5 Nov 2026 — guidance tracker), on the core air-conditioning business beating plan through high-value-added products, pricing and cost-down despite Middle East, tariff and materials headwinds; otherwise the stock tracked its sector with no dominant single event.

One of the larger mid-table upgrades: the OP guide was raised twice to ¥88,000mn (+41.9%, latest 10 Nov 2026 — guidance tracker), on AI-driven capex for advanced semiconductors and data centres in the factory-automation business and firm healthcare demand.

No guidance event at all: the OP guide was held at ¥110,000mn all year with zero revisions (guidance tracker), so the gain is honestly a sector/market read-across — the stock rose with TOPIX and the machinery complex rather than on any company-specific catalyst.

Headline OP guidance was left unchanged at ¥75,000mn, but business profit was raised to ¥95,000mn (+5.6%, 29 Oct 2026 — guidance tracker), with the OP line held only because of a loss on the European automotive-business transfer; the modest beat of TOPIX is consistent with that mixed revision.

The joint-largest upgrade in the tracker — the OP guide doubled across three revisions to ¥52,000mn (+100.0%, latest 13 Nov 2026 — guidance tracker), on industrial-machinery orders beating assumptions amid AI semiconductor capex and a weaker yen — yet the share return was only mid-table, i.e. the upgrades were absorbed without a re-rating to the top of the table.

A single late OP guide raise to ¥103,000mn (+8.4%, 6 Nov 2026 — guidance tracker), made inside the Q2 tanshin with no separate stated reason, broadly explains a return only slightly ahead of TOPIX; no dominant corporate event was found.

No revision event: the FY8/27 OP guide of ¥15,600mn was set on 15 Oct 2026 and left unchanged, with the next print not due until January 2027 (guidance tracker); the return is essentially TOPIX-matching (+1.2pt over 12M) and is honestly a market read-across.

The OP guide was raised once, early, to ¥26,000mn (+36.8%, 5 Aug 2026 — guidance tracker), after the company lifted its order forecast to ¥276,000mn on aerospace, defence, data-centre/energy and semiconductor-equipment demand; the return nonetheless only matched TOPIX, so the upgrade was largely absorbed by mid-year.

The OP guide was raised once to ¥7,400mn (+19.4%, 4 Nov 2026 — guidance tracker) with a dividend raise, on strong semiconductor demand for high-purity phosphoric acid and compound-semiconductor materials; the negative YTD shows the gain was made in late 2025 and faded in 2026 despite the raise.

Two OP guide raises to ¥585,000mn (+15.2%, latest 29 Oct 2026 — guidance tracker), on construction-machinery demand beating assumptions in many regions in H1 plus a weaker yen, produced a return almost exactly in line with TOPIX (−0.1pt over 12M) — a solid revision story fully matched by the market.

No guidance revision: the FY3/27 OP guide of ¥12,200mn (+6.9% YoY), set 12 May 2026, was reaffirmed unchanged at H1 (5 Nov 2026), with H1 OP progress at 55.0% of the guide and a buyback of up to 2,000,000 shares / ¥7,000mn (resolved 12 May 2026) running — the name tracked the warehousing/logistics sector rather than any single event (warehousing data file 9303.md; not in the guidance tracker).

A large but low-quality upgrade: the OP guide was raised once to ¥400,000mn (+33.3%, 4 Aug 2026 — guidance tracker), with the company citing yen weakness and an expected US tariff refund, partly offset by Middle East raw-material costs — FX/refund rather than volume — which fits a return slightly behind TOPIX.

A single, very late OP guide raise to ¥294,000mn (+34.2%, 13 Nov 2026 — guidance tracker), on recent order trends and revised FX assumptions, came too late in the window to lift the full-year return, which finished slightly behind TOPIX.

A mixed revision: adjusted OP guidance was raised twice to ¥710,000mn (+20.3%, latest 30 Oct 2026 — guidance tracker) on FA systems and air-conditioning/appliances, but net income guidance was cut to ¥465,000mn on an expected ~¥100,000mn impairment from transferring 50% of the automotive-equipment business to the Hon Hai group; the flat YTD reflects that mix.

Two OP guide raises to ¥240,700mn (+13.4%, latest 23 Oct 2026 — guidance tracker, with only generic company wording on the reasons) did not hold the stock in 2026: the 12M gain was made in 2025 and the YTD return is −12.2%, a de-rating against the FA/robotics complex despite the revisions.

The driver is an OP guide **cut**: on 30 Oct 2026 revenue guidance was raised to ¥290,000mn but OP was cut from ¥17,500mn to ¥15,500mn (−11.4%, calculation) mainly for M&A advisory/PMI costs on the Hankyu Hanshin Express acquisition announced the same day (warehousing data file 9301.md; not in the guidance tracker) — consistent with a return behind TOPIX, partly cushioned by ongoing buybacks.

Two raises in adjusted OP guidance to ¥1,450,000mn (+10.3%, latest 28 Oct 2026 — guidance tracker), led by Energy and Connective Industries, still left the shares well behind TOPIX (−8.8pt over 12M): no single negative event was found, and the lag is honestly a large-cap de-rating against its own revision pace.

Disco gives no full-year guidance (one-quarter-ahead outlook only — guidance tracker; latest Apr–Dec 2026 cumulative OP outlook ¥174,700mn, 22 Oct 2026), so there was no revision catalyst, and the stock lagged the semiconductor-equipment leaders it usually trades with.

A substantial OP guide upgrade — raised twice to ¥56,000mn (+33.3%, latest 29 Oct 2026 — guidance tracker), on semiconductor-equipment and machine-tool demand in Industrial Machinery plus a weaker yen — was barely rewarded: the return is near-flat, suggesting the bearing sector's auto exposure and the pending NTN integration (NSK's own integration cost ~¥5.0bn, per the NTN briefing in company-attribution.md) capped the re-rating.

The OP guide was raised to ¥32,600mn (+17.7%, 31 Jul 2026, with no company-stated reason extracted — guidance tracker) and left unchanged at Q3, yet the shares ended flat over 12M and down YTD; no dominant event was found, and the honest read is that the upgrade was fully discounted early.

The tracker's only outright OP cut: guidance was cut to ¥23,000mn (−9.8%, 5 Nov 2026 — guidance tracker) on Environment-segment profitability deterioration (Inova order delays and additional project costs), with ordinary profit and net income held on better FX — a flat share price is the unsurprising result.

A modest OP guide raise to ¥123,000mn (+7.0%, 30 Oct 2026 — guidance tracker), on maintained price spreads and high-value-added products with an assumed H2 payback from H1 pull-forward, was not enough to move the shares, which finished flat.

No guidance event: the OP guide of ¥9,012mn (set 14 Aug 2026) was unchanged at Q1 FY6/27 (16 Nov 2026 — guidance tracker), and no dominant corporate event was found; the small decline is a no-news drift behind TOPIX.

Counter-intuitively, the OP guide was raised twice to ¥30,000mn (+33.3%, latest 4 Aug 2026 — guidance tracker), on strong global orders and a weaker yen against the euro, yet the shares fell slightly; no company-specific negative was found, so the honest driver is that the upgrades were discounted and the name tracked the weaker end of the machine-tool complex.
A small, late OP guide raise to ¥128,000mn (+6.7%, 6 Nov 2026, no company-stated reason extracted — guidance tracker) did not offset the year's de-rating; no dominant single event was found.

A governance shock wrapped around flawless fundamentals: the shares peaked at $243.37 on 6 Oct 2026, Jensen Huang resigned on 12 Nov, a perfect print (Q3 revenue $115.8bn, +103%; Q4 guide $130bn ±3%) could not hold the complex, reports of an SEC accounting examination took the shares to $125.53 on 20 Nov (−48% from the high), and Huang's unanimous reinstatement on 23 Nov drove a +31.5% rebound to $165.05 — twelve months containing a halving and a resurrection net out to −7.2%.

OP guidance was held at ¥125,000mn all year (0.0%), even as net income guidance was raised +14.9% and the orders plan was lifted repeatedly to ¥1,295,000mn by Q3 (13 Nov 2026 — guidance tracker); with no OP upgrade in a year of upgrades, the shares lagged.

A substantial OP guide raise to ¥365,000mn (+23.7%, 30 Oct 2026 — guidance tracker), on AI data-centre component demand beating the April assumptions, came after most of the 12M decline had already happened; the positive YTD (+2.6%) shows the stock stabilising into the raise rather than being driven by it all year.

Record nine-month orders (+56.5%), a record backlog (¥929,400mn), an OP guide raise to ¥119,000mn (+13.3%, latest 11 Nov 2026 — guidance tracker) and a ¥40bn buyback still left the shares −43.6% below the May peak, because OP margin fell 0.4pt to 15.1% on +13.9% revenue and one stated raise reason was revenue pull-forward — a multiple story.

A 4.2% H1 OP margin met a merger bill: ¥4.4bn of NSK-integration costs absorbed the entire OP improvement (the OP guide was held at ¥33,000mn, revenue only raised, 30 Oct 2026 — guidance tracker), ~¥4.0bn of the cost lands in H2, and the mid-term plan's ¥50bn OP target is an explicit miss.

The universe's clearest execution failure and one of only two OP cuts in the tracker: the OP guide was cut to ¥57,500mn (−4.2%, 9 Oct 2026 — guidance tracker) on a core-system migration that disrupted production and shipments, even as revenue guidance was raised and Q2 orders were a record (AC servo orders +76%); H1 delivered only 38.4% of the cut guide, so H2 needs an 11.3% OP margin against 7.7% in H1.

The governance name: a second consecutive audit disclaimer, a ¥632.1bn impairment, ~¥160.7bn of cumulative inappropriate-accounting impact, TSE Special Attention status, and Q1/Q2 tanshin formally postponed with the interim-report deadline extended to 16 Dec 2026 (guidance tracker: the FY3/27 OP ¥200,000mn plan was published 30 Sep 2026 under the disclaimer and is unverified) — the discount is a listing-risk discount, not a demand view.

The same optical story as Furukawa — H1 records and the OP guide raised twice to ¥500,000mn (+17.6%, latest 30 Oct 2026 — guidance tracker), with a 4-for-1 split (1 Jul 2026, adjusted) — dragged by the largest business: automotive harnesses (57.4% of FY3/26 revenue) saw H1 OP fall −17.7% on Middle East volume loss and copper costs, the raised guide needs ¥280.4bn of OP in H2, and the cable complex de-rated as a group from June.

Headline H1 OP rose +65.6%, but ¥42.6bn of it was real-estate sale gains, and the raised ¥270,000mn OP guide (+12.5%, latest 4 Nov 2026 — guidance tracker) contains ¥93bn of property gains (OP ex-gains ¥177bn); H1 orders fell −12.8% against a ¥1,890bn full-year orders guide, and the market is capitalising the ex-property line.

The rise was fundamentals (H1 OP a record ¥235bn, +161%; a 6-for-1 split on 1 Apr 2026 is adjusted and explains none of the fall); the turn was the 10 Nov 2026 print — despite the record half, Fujikura made its first downward full-year revision of the year, cutting implied H2 OP by ~¥40bn to ¥194bn, of which only ~¥3–7bn is explained by FX on the analyses found, and the company's own stated reason is 未取得; the shares fell −12.2% in the 20 Nov crash to the ¥2,252 trough. (Fujikura has no chain in the guidance tracker — see notes.)

The clearest company-specific driver in the report: a ~¥200bn international offering and convertible issue in July 2026 (37,350,000 new shares at ¥2,609) for aero-engine, turbine, robotics and hydrogen capex — the shares fell more than 7% on the first reports (1 Jul); H1 was a record and business-profit guidance rose to ¥185,000mn (+8.8% — guidance tracker), but the beat leaned on a tariff refund, a litigation settlement and FX, and defence orders fell −64% YoY. A 5-for-1 split (1 Apr 2026) is adjusted.

Earnings grew only modestly — the FY3/27 OP guide was raised only to ¥24,000mn on 6 Nov 2026 (from ¥23,000mn, +4.3% by calculation; warehousing data file 9302.md — not in the guidance tracker) — in a year when most guided companies raised far more; February's Mitsui Fudosan alliance issued 3,000,000 new shares (~4% dilution), partly offset by buybacks (¥8,641mn spent in H1 against a ¥34,000mn facility).

The peak was the war spike (2 Mar 2026, the first Tokyo session after the strikes on Iran began; all three heavy-industry names peaked that day) and the fade came despite a record H1 (orders ¥3,612.5bn; business profit +45.3%), a sharp guidance raise on 6 Nov 2026 (business profit ¥540,000mn → ¥600,000mn, +11.1% — guidance tracker) and a ¥300bn buyback: the market is pricing defence orders down −64% YoY in H1 and a ~¥90bn IGCC warranty charge inside Q2 — an expectations unwind, not an earnings decline.

blocks.heading: 6. Top movers — the reasons
blocks.html: Advantech (2395 TW, +106.7%). The order book did it: record 3Q26 revenue NT$32,440mn (+83% YoY), operating profit +151%, and a consolidated book-to-bill of 1.64 (North America 2.12) with bookings up five straight quarters. The 4Q outlook (US$970–990mn) was framed by management itself as conservative against a record October. The fade from NT$740 (5 Oct) to NT$589 is the complex-wide autumn de-rating; no company-specific negative disclosure was found. Furukawa Electric (5801, +100.3%). H1 operating profit tripled to ¥57.6bn (+201.1%) as Optical Solutions swung from ¥0.7bn to ¥23.6bn of OP; guidance was raised twice to ¥136,000mn (+43.2%). The stock still fell −69.9% from its ¥6,014 peak (26 May): −17.1% on 5 Nov alone, a Goldman Sachs target cut (¥6,400 → ¥4,100, 8 Nov), and the desk's open question — how much of the 0.8% → 18.0% optical margin is shortage pricing that reverses when industry fibre capacity lands in 2027–28. Misumi (9962, +65.6%). H1 OP +89.8% (margin 9.5% → 13.6%) on data-centre demand and the digital-model initiatives; guidance raised twice to ¥78,000mn (+41.8%); ¥15,909mn of H1 buybacks and a dividend raise alongside. Its 11 Nov peak was set on the eve of the crash — the 12M gain is an earnings-revision story, not momentum. Ryohin Keikaku (7453, +62.5%). A record FY8/26 (OP ¥103,436mn, +40.1%, the first time above ¥100bn) and a FY8/27 guide to the first ¥1tn revenue year. The year's one negative is post-peak: the MUJI online store has been suspended since 6 Nov after an unauthorised-access incident (up to ~27.26mn records potentially exposed); the earnings cost is unquantified and the guidance predates the suspension. Harmonic Drive (6324, +50.6%). Guidance +64.5% to ¥10,200mn — but off a FY3/26 OP base of just ¥2,568mn. The ¥8,890 July peak and the −52.6% round trip are multiple expansion and compression on a very small profit base; no guidance cut or negative disclosure was found. Tokyo Electron (8035, +43.8%). H1 OP +67.2%; the first full-year guide (disclosed only on 30 Oct) put FY3/27 OP at ¥1,169,000mn (+87.1%), with management framing CY2027 wafer-fab equipment at $210bn or more; a ¥150bn buyback accompanied the print. The −43.2% from the 1 Jul peak is the sector path, not a miss. Advantest (6857, +43.0%). H1 OP ¥456.8bn (+96.5%, at a 54.0% margin); guidance +54.1% to ¥967,000mn on CPU-testing demand from agentic AI — 'a third layer of growth on top of GPUs and custom ASICs' (company Q&A, 28 Oct 2026); a ¥280bn buyback with the print. It was also the crash's purest round trip: −11.1% on 16 Nov, the largest single Nikkei drag on 17 Nov, and more than +14% in the 24 Nov rebound. FUJI (6134, +42.5%). Robot Solutions (SMT mounters) drove H1 OP +250.6%; guidance +50.2% to ¥65,500mn; a ¥10bn buyback completed on 6 Nov, with cancellation on 14 Dec. Visibility is the caveat: backlog of ¥80,472mn is only ~3.8 months of guided sales. Sodick (6143, +42.5%). The guide doubled (+100.0%) on China EDM demand and AI-related injection-moulding machines, beating the 2029 mid-term targets three years early; a ~¥8.8bn secondary offering (a cross-shareholding unwind) was the autumn supply overhang, partly offset by a ¥3bn buyback. Keyence (6861, +36.4%). No guidance by policy, so the 29 Oct print was the event: H1 sales +34.9%, OP +50.0% at a 55.5% margin, with a 5-for-1 split and a dividend raise announced the same day. Whether +34.9% growth is a spike or a step-up is the desk's stated open question.

blocks.heading: 7. Bottom movers — the reasons, and the NVIDIA round trip
blocks.html: Mitsubishi Heavy Industries (7011, −27.4%). The peak was the war spike — all three heavy-industry names peaked on 2 Mar 2026, the first Tokyo session after the strikes on Iran began — and the fade happened despite a record H1 (orders ¥3,612.5bn; business profit +45.3%), a sharp guidance raise on 6 Nov (business profit ¥540bn → ¥600bn) and a ¥300bn buyback. The market is pricing what the same print showed: defence orders −64% YoY in H1, and a ~¥90bn IGCC warranty charge inside Q2. This is an expectations unwind, not an earnings decline. Mitsui-Soko HD (9302, −20.7%). Earnings grew modestly (the FY3/27 OP guide was raised only to ¥24,000mn on 6 Nov) in a year when 44 of 50 guided companies raised; February's Mitsui Fudosan alliance issued 3,000,000 new shares (~4% dilution), partly offset by buybacks. J-Core's own initiation (24 Nov) rates the name Overweight at ¥3,800 on the real-estate NAV — the market's verdict and the desk's differ, and Section 11 says what would close the gap. Kawasaki Heavy (7012, −20.3%). The clearest company-specific driver in this report: a ~¥200bn international offering and convertible issue in July (37,350,000 new shares at ¥2,609) for aero-engine, turbine, robotics and hydrogen capex — the shares fell more than 7% on the first reports (1 Jul). H1 was a record and guidance rose again, but the beat leaned on a tariff refund, a litigation settlement and FX, and defence orders fell −64% YoY. Fujikura (5803, −16.5%). The rise was fundamentals (H1 OP a record ¥235bn, +161%); the turn was the 10 Nov print — despite the record half, Fujikura made its first downward full-year revision of the year, cutting implied H2 operating profit by ~¥40bn to ¥194bn, of which only ~¥3–7bn is explained by FX on the analyses found; the company's own stated reason is 未取得. The shares fell −12.2% in the 20 Nov crash to the ¥2,252 trough. IHI (7013, −14.4%). Headline H1 OP rose +65.6% — but ¥42.6bn of it was real-estate sale gains, and the raised ¥270,000mn guide contains ¥93bn of property gains (OP ex-gains: ¥177bn); H1 orders fell −12.8% against a ¥1,890bn full-year orders guide. The market is capitalising the ex-property line. Sumitomo Electric (5802, −13.6%). The same optical story as Furukawa — H1 records, guidance raised twice to ¥500,000mn — dragged by the largest business: automotive harnesses (57.4% of FY3/26 revenue) saw H1 OP fall −17.7% on Middle East volume loss and copper costs, and the raised guide needs ¥280.4bn of OP in H2. The cable complex de-rated as a group from June. Nidec (6594, −11.9%). The governance name: a second consecutive audit disclaimer, a ¥632.1bn impairment, ~¥160.7bn of cumulative inappropriate-accounting impact, TSE Special Attention status, and Q1/Q2 tanshin formally postponed, with the interim-report deadline extended to 16 Dec 2026. The discount is a listing-risk discount, not a demand view. Yaskawa (6506, −10.7%; the worst YTD at −27.5%). The universe's clearest execution failure: one of only two operating-profit cuts in the tracker (¥60,000mn → ¥57,500mn, 9 Oct; the other cut was Kanadevia), on a core-system migration that disrupted production and shipments — while Q2 orders were a record (AC servo orders +76%). H1 delivered only 38.4% of the cut guide, so H2 needs an 11.3% OP margin against 7.7% in H1. NTN (6472, −9.4%). A 4.2% H1 OP margin met a merger bill: ¥4.4bn of NSK-integration costs absorbed the entire OP improvement (the guide was held at ¥33,000mn), ~¥4.0bn of the cost lands in H2, and the mid-term plan's ¥50bn OP target is an explicit miss. Daifuku (6383, −9.4%). Record nine-month orders (+56.5%), a record backlog, a guidance raise and a ¥40bn buyback — and a −43.6% fall from the May peak, because OP margin fell 0.4pt to 15.1% on +13.9% revenue and one stated raise reason was revenue pull-forward. A multiple story, addressed in Section 10. NVIDIA (NVDA, −7.2% in USD). A governance shock wrapped around flawless fundamentals: $243.37 on 6 Oct; Huang's resignation (12 Nov); a perfect print (Q3 revenue $115.8bn, +103%; Q4 guide $130bn ±3%) that could not hold the complex; reports of an SEC accounting examination took the shares to $125.53 on 20 Nov (−48% from the high); reinstatement on 23 Nov returned +31.5% in a day. Twelve months that contained a halving and a resurrection net out to −7.2%.

blocks.heading: 8. Earnings seasons — the fundamental backdrop
blocks.html: FY3/26 — a record season. Aggregate net profit for the FY3/26 season was ¥54.71tn, +9.0% YoY and a record high (SMBC Nikko tally of 1,116 TOPIX March year-end companies, via Jiji Press, 22 May 2026); AI/semiconductor and data-centre names and the banks led, transportation equipment fell on US tariffs. Company guidance for FY3/27 was set at ¥63.33tn of net profit, +8.3% (same tally) — deliberately conservative underneath: on Nomura's tally, aggregate recurring-profit guidance was only +1.9% and 76% of companies guided below consensus, mainly on ¥150–152/USD FX assumptions. The FY3/26 aggregate recurring-profit total itself is 未取得. Buybacks set the tone for returns: announced frames reached ¥25.7tn in calendar 2026 by 13 Nov (Nomura tally), with Jan–May frames of ¥16.2tn, +34% YoY, a record for the period (Nikkei tally). Q1 FY3/27 — the profit surge. Aggregate net profit rose +65% YoY to ¥19.77tn (Nikkei tally, Aug 2026); roughly 80% of sectors grew profit, one company in four posted a record quarter, and about 20% of companies raised full-year net-profit guidance already at Q1. An operating-profit aggregate for the quarter is 未取得. H1 FY3/27 — the record that frames November. Aggregate H1 net profit was a record ¥35.75tn, +26% YoY (Nikkei tally of 1,028 TSE Prime companies) — the sixth consecutive record first half. Electrical equipment net profit rose +96% and supplied roughly 40% of manufacturing's profit increase; Kioxia's net profit was ¥2.19tn (37×) and Advantest's more than doubled to ¥368bn. Guidance breadth was decisively positive: 633 companies raised full-year recurring-profit guidance against 197 cuts (Nomura, 17 Nov 2026), and 369 raised net-profit guidance against 74 cuts on SMBC Nikko's count. The one soft spot: Q2 alone (Jul–Sep) fell −3% YoY on the Nikkei tally, driven by energy-cost sectors — electric utilities swung to a ¥145.2bn net loss — not by the AI complex. The read-across is the point of this section: no aggregate earnings deterioration preceded the November fall. The crash re-priced positioning on top of record earnings, which is why Section 1 calls it a positioning accident, and why the Part 5 view treats the de-rating of the guidance raisers as stock-specific opportunity rather than a cycle turn.

blocks.heading: Part 4 — The US comparison block and the yen
9. The US: a defensive year — and Japan outperformed
blocks.html: The US was the control group that proves the year was Japan-specific. The S&P 500 returned +6.43% over 12M and +5.19% YTD (7,201.09 on 24 Nov), the Dow +6.17% / +4.07% (closing above 50,000), and the Nasdaq Composite only +3.07% / +2.11% — a growth index lagging its own market. Sector leadership (Select Sector SPDR ETFs, labelled proxies) was defensive and value-tilted: Energy +36.44% far ahead, then Consumer Staples +17.70%, Health Care +16.34% and Materials +14.27%; Technology +12.02% beat the index but was only mid-pack; Communication Services −8.62% / −11.27% was the clear laggard and explains the Nasdaq's underperformance. The best-to-worst sector spread was 45.1pt — wide, but Japan's was wider (76.2pt between Marine Transportation and Other Products on the to-October basis). The yen barely moved across the year as a whole — USD/JPY 156.94 → 159.01 (+1.32%, a modestly weaker yen) — which conceals the year's real FX story: a January month-end of 153.16, a slide to 162.63 by June, the 22 Jul intraday print of 163.988 (a 40-year yen low), and the ¥15.39tn intervention of 30 Jul–3 Aug that pulled the rate back into the 157–159 range. For a yen-based investor, FX added only ~1–2pt to US returns across the full windows — far less than in the large yen-swing years. Cross-country (local currency): Taiwan's TAIEX +49.09% and Korea's KOSPI +29.76% rode the same AI-capex cycle as Japan's electrical complex, while Hong Kong fell −14.19% and the Shanghai Composite −8.31%. Japan's +14.40% (TOPIX) sits between the AI-beta markets and the US — earned, unusually, alongside a rising policy rate.

blocks.heading: 10. Laggards with a credible catch-up catalyst
blocks.html: Daifuku (6383) — the cleanest catch-up candidate. The de-rating (−43.6% from the peak) prices margin dilution and pull-forward, but the order book is a fact: nine-month orders +56.5%, backlog a record ¥929,400mn, guidance raised, and a ¥40bn buyback running to 31 Jan 2027. Watch: (1) Q4 OP margin against the 15.1% nine-month print; (2) Clean Factomation order pace in Q4; (3) whether the FY2027 guide converts backlog at better than 15% margins. Yaskawa (6506) — a conversion test, with a date. Demand is not the question (record Q2 orders; AC servo +76%); the system migration is. H2 must deliver an 11.3% OP margin against 7.7% in H1. Watch: (1) the Q3 print (Feb 2027) for shipment normalisation; (2) Robotics segment margin against Fanuc's robot growth (+12.6%) — the share-loss question; (3) any second guidance revision. If H2 converts, the −27.5% YTD is the entry the order book argues for; if it does not, the cut was the first of two. Mitsubishi Heavy (7011) — expectations have reset; the buyback is live. The shares now price defence-order timing, not the March war premium, while the company raised its business-profit guide to ¥600bn and is buying back ¥300bn (to Nov 2027). Watch: (1) H2 defence order intake against the ¥1,800bn full-year segment guide (H1: ¥153.8bn); (2) GTCC order momentum; (3) any further IGCC-type charges. Fujikura (5803) — conditional, not clean. At −69.2% from the peak the shares price the H2 cut as a demand turn; if it was prudence, Q3 re-rates them. Watch: (1) the Q3 print against the implied ¥194bn of H2 OP; (2) the company's stated reason for the cut, still 未取得; (3) US data-centre regulatory signals, the cited H2 mix risk. We do not call this a catch-up until (2) is answered.

blocks.heading: 11. Cheap for a reason
blocks.html: Nidec (6594) — no catch-up call until the filings land. The discount is about whether the accounts can be believed: two consecutive disclaimers, restatements that roughly halved five years of cumulative reported OP, and a first half whose results have never been published. The single date that matters is 16 Dec 2026, the extended interim-report deadline; the ¥103.0bn Nidec Components sale to Carlyle (closing 1 Dec) funds the pivot but does not repair disclosure. IHI (7013) — the guide is not the earnings. ¥93bn of the ¥270,000mn OP guide is property gains; ex-gains OP of ¥177bn is the number to capitalise, and H1 orders fell −12.8% against a ¥1,890bn guide. Cheap on headline OP, not on the ex-gains line. Kawasaki Heavy (7012) — dilution absorbed, orders not yet. The ~¥200bn raise strengthened the balance sheet (JCR upgraded the name to A+ on 28 Oct) but defence orders fell −64% YoY in H1 against a ¥450.5bn full-year guide; the catch-up requires the H2 order print, not patience. NTN (6472) — the merger bill is still arriving. ~¥4.0bn of the ¥4.4bn NSK-integration cost lands in H2, the mid-term OP target (¥50bn) is conceded missed, and Europe is loss-making; the 1 Oct 2027 integration is a 2027 story, not a catch-up catalyst for this fiscal year. Mitsui-Soko HD (9302) — the exception that proves the rule. Earnings will not close this gap (low-single-digit OP growth); the asset side might: rental real-estate unrealised gains of ¥102,140mn are ~72% of equity, and J-Core's ¥3,800 target (Overweight, 24 Nov) is an NAV argument. The catalyst to watch is capital policy — buyback pace (¥8,641mn spent in H1 against a ¥34,000mn facility) and any move on the property portfolio — not the quarterly P&L.

blocks.heading: 12. Leaders — who still has legs, who is extended
blocks.html: Still has legs — Advantest (6857) and Tokyo Electron (8035). Both de-rated 35–43% from their peaks into the crash while raising guidance (+54.1%, and a first-time guide at +87.1% respectively), both are buying back stock (¥280bn; ¥150bn), and the demand frame is dated and checkable: TEL's CY2027 wafer-fab equipment market of $210bn or more. Watch: (1) October machinery orders (16 Dec) and the Q3 prints; (2) Advantest's SoC tester share and capacity bring-forward; (3) China mix (36.4% of TEL's Q2 sales) against export-control headlines. Misumi (9962) belongs in the same group on revision momentum (+41.8% and still rising into the October print) — watch monthly sales and the FA segment's data-centre exposure. Advantech (2395) has the order cover (book-to-bill 1.64) to defend its +106.7%, with management's own 'conservative' 4Q framing as the tell; watch monthly revenue against the US$970–990mn guide. Extended — Harmonic Drive (6324). A +64.5% guidance raise sounds like cover until the base is stated: FY3/27E OP of ¥10,200mn is roughly 4× a ¥2,568mn print, and the shares have already round-tripped ¥8,890 → ¥4,216 once. The multiple, not the orders, is the risk in both directions. Furukawa Electric (5801) — +100.3% on the year, and still the desk's open question: an 18.0% optical margin earned in a shortage is worth less than one earned in balance, and Goldman's target cut to ¥4,100 (8 Nov) says the street is split. Watch Optical Solutions' margin in Q3 and any 2027 fibre-capacity announcements. Ryohin Keikaku (7453) — a record year is priced; the unquantified EC suspension (the online store has been closed since 6 Nov, with no reopening date) is not. The 13 Jan 2027 Q1 print is the first number that can settle it. FUJI (6134) — +50.2% of guidance upgrades against ~3.8 months of backlog visibility: the multiple assumes the AI-server mounter cycle extends; watch order intake, not the P&L. Update (enrichment, 25 Nov 2026). The corrected June record and the −22.0% Nikkei drawdown deepen, but do not change, the Part 5 calls above: the fall from the record was a positioning unwind on record earnings (H1 net profit +26%), and the breadth data — only 24 of 52 comparable coverage names beat TOPIX over 12M — confirm a two-tier market in which the catch-up candidates named above remain stock-specific, not beta, trades.

blocks.html: Basis. All returns are price returns (dividends excluded) computed from closing levels. Japan: TOPIX and TOPIX-33 from JPX Monthly Statistics Reports; the Nikkei 225 from Yahoo Finance ^N225 (cross-checked against press closes); coverage companies from the in-house price files (Yahoo Finance closes), with per-name peak and trough data in the working papers. US sectors are Select Sector SPDR ETF price returns, used as labelled proxies for S&P 500 sector indices, not index total returns. Gap 1 — TOPIX-33 at 24 Nov 2026: 未取得 (all 33 sectors). JPX's November 2026 Monthly Statistics Report (sections 3-5(1)/(2), day-24 rows) is expected in the first business days of December 2026, and the sector block will be completed from it. No proxy was substituted: no TSE ETF tracks the TOPIX-33 sectors (the NEXT FUNDS 1617–1633 series tracks TOPIX-17). Gap 2 — CSI 300: 未取得 (the Yahoo series returned a single data point); the Shanghai Composite is used for China. Gap 3 — Fujikura's company-stated reason for its ~¥40bn H2 OP cut (10 Nov 2026): 未取得; only commentary on the presentation materials was found. Gap 4 — Ryohin Keikaku's EC-suspension earnings impact: not quantified by the company as of 16 Nov 2026. Correction to the in-house record (revised in the 25 Nov 2026 enrichment). The window's highest Nikkei close was 72,366.34 on 25 Jun 2026 (Asahi Shimbun/Jiji, Jun 2026; Reuters poll, 25 Nov 2026), not 70,683.98 on 6 Oct 2026: that was a secondary high, on the day TOPIX made its own peak close of 4,183.56. The peak-to-trough Nikkei drawdown to 56,436.65 on 20 Nov 2026 is therefore −22.0%, not −20.2%. An earlier draft of this report — and the correction paragraph it replaces — put the peak on 6 Oct because the daily-series pull behind the index levels was defective for June 2026; a fresh pull shows closes of 71,250.06 (19 Jun), 72,353.96 (22 Jun) and 72,366.34 (25 Jun), all above the October level. The same archive file's 'October peak of 61,142' is the close of 13 Nov 2026 (61,142.35), the pre-crash reference level. This report follows the corrected daily series throughout. NVIDIA's in-house series ends on 23 Nov 2026; its +31.5% reinstatement session is the window's final close for that name. Advantech (2395) is Taiwan-listed and TWD-denominated.
